black.overview: Black is a color that results from the absence or complete absorption of visible light. It is an achromatic color, without chroma, like white and grey. It is often used symbolically or figuratively to represent darkness. Black and white have often been used to describe opposites such as good and evil, the Dark Ages versus the Age of Enlightenment, and night versus day. Since the Middle Ages, black has been the symbolic color of solemnity and authority, and for this reason it is still commonly worn by judges and magistrates. Black was one of the first colors used by artists in Neolithic cave paintings. It was used in ancient Egypt and Greece as the color of the underworld.

butterfly.overview: Butterflies are winged insects from the lepidopteran superfamily Papilionoidea, characterised by large, often brightly coloured wings that often fold together when at rest, and a conspicuous, fluttering flight. The oldest butterfly fossils have been dated to the Paleocene, about 56 million years ago, though molecular evidence suggests that they likely originated in the Cretaceous. As holometabolous insects, butterflies undergo complete metamorphosis, meaning that their life cycle comprises four stages. Winged adults lay eggs on plant foliage on which their larvae, known as caterpillars, will feed.

Fergus carved a dummy wooden sword to disguise the fact he was unarmed. Ailill returns the sword to him before the final battle, and Fergus speaks a poem over it, calling it Caladcholc in one version, and Caladbolg in another. excalibur.overview: King Arthur's sword: given to him by the Lady of the Lake in some tellings, drawn from a stone in others, and thrown back into the water when he lies dying. A Welsh weapon called Caledfwlch became Geoffrey of Monmouth's Caliburnus and the French Escalibor, and through them the most famous sword in Western legend.wpgeoffrey

article.html:
Most swords in legend are famous for what they kill. Excalibur is famous for where it comes from and where it goes. It rises out of a lake in a woman's hand, and in the end a hand takes it back. Between those two moments lies a whole reign. The sword is less a weapon than a lease on power, granted by the Otherworld and returned when the time is up.

That is why the most memorable Excalibur scene is not a battle but a hesitation. Dying, Arthur asks Bedivere to throw the sword into the water, and Bedivere cannot do it. He hides it, lies, hides it again. The best of swords seems too precious to waste. Only when Arthur rebukes him does he throw it, and the lake answers. The scene is about letting go, and it gives grief a gesture: the king has to give back the thing that made him king.

The sword in the stone tells the opposite story, about taking hold. Nobody can draw it but the true king, a boy no one expected. The test cannot be cheated, bought or forced. Later storytellers could not resist joining the two scenes, so that one sword stands for both the claim and its surrender. In Malory they are separate, and the separation matters: the stone sword proves who Arthur is; Excalibur, from the lake, is what he is given to do.

Excalibur is also older than its stories. Behind it stand a Welsh Caledfwlch, an Irish Caladbolg, and the thousands of real swords that people in prehistoric Europe broke, bent or laid in lakes and rivers. Whether or not the romances remember those offerings, they share the same intuition: that the finest things belong in the end to the waters and the gods, not to us.

For a storyteller, Excalibur is a model of how to give an object a life: an origin that is a gift, a rule that binds the owner, a theft (Morgan's taking of the scabbard), and a return.

debates.h: Is the sword in the stone Excalibur?
debates.html:
• The same sword. In Robert de Boron and the Vulgate Merlin, the sword Arthur draws from the stone is Excalibur.wp
  • Two swords. In the Post-Vulgate and Malory, the stone sword breaks and Excalibur comes later from the Lady of the Lake.malory1
  • Merged in modern memory. Film and fiction usually blend the two scenes into one sword.wp

debates.h: Where does the name come from?
debates.html:
• Welsh Caledfwlch. The Welsh name came first, and Geoffrey Latinised it.wp
  • A Celtic sword-name shared with Ireland. It is often compared with Caladbolg, the sword of the Irish hero Fergus mac Róich. Whether one borrowed from the other, or both come from an older word, is debated.wpwp:Caladbolg
  • Latin influence. Geoffrey's Caliburnus may also echo Latin chalybs, "steel".wp

debates.h: Did a real custom lie behind the lake?
debates.html:
• Yes, a memory of votive offerings. Archaeologists have found many weapons deliberately placed in water across prehistoric Britain and Europe.wp:Llyn Cerrig Bach
  • Not necessarily. The scene can be explained as literary invention, centuries after such offerings ended; the link is suggestive, not proven.wp

Some scholars see a memory of such offerings in the sword returned to the lake.wpwp:Llyn Cerrig Bach

Twelfth-century Tuscany has its own sword in a rock, still at the chapel of Montesiepi, attributed to the knight-turned-hermit Galgano Guidotti.wpwp:Galgano Guidotti

myth.html:
In the Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, Arthur lists the few things he will not give away: his ship, his mantle, his sword Caledfwlch, his spear Rhongomyniad, his shield, his dagger Carnwennan and his wife Gwenhwyfar. The name is usually read as "hard notch" or "hard breach".culhwchwp

Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin History of the Kings of Britain (c. 1136) calls it Caliburnus, "the best of swords, forged in the Isle of Avalon", and gives Arthur victory with it over the Saxons. French romance turned the name into Escalibor.geoffreywp

The two great scenes come later. In Robert de Boron's Merlin (c. 1200) the boy Arthur proves his right to the throne by drawing a sword from a stone that no grown knight can move. In the Post-Vulgate romances and in Malory, that sword breaks in a fight, and Merlin takes Arthur to a lake where an arm clothed in white samite holds a sword above the water: Excalibur, the gift of the Lady of the Lake. Merlin tells him the scabbard is worth ten of the sword, for while he wears it he will lose no blood. Morgan le Fay later steals the scabbard.malory1wp

At the end, wounded at Camlann, Arthur orders a knight (Girflet in the French Death of Arthur, Bedivere in Malory) to throw the sword into the lake. Twice the knight hides it, unable to waste so fine a thing; the third time he throws it, and a hand rises, catches it, brandishes it three times and draws it under.malory2wp

seen.h: Medieval: a gift and a trust
seen.html: In the romances the sword is not Arthur's property but a loan. It comes from the Otherworld (the Lake, Avalon) and must go back there; Arthur's reign is legitimate while he holds it rightly. Merlin's remark that the scabbard is worth more than the sword teaches that protection matters more than conquest.malory1

modun.overview: Modu (c. 234–174 BCE) was the son of Touman and the founder of the empire of the Xiongnu. He came to power by ordering his men to kill his father in 209 BCE. Modu ruled from 209 to 174 BCE. He was a military leader under his father Touman and later chanyu of the Xiongnu Empire, based on the Mongolian Plateau. He secured the throne and established a powerful Xiongnu Empire by successfully unifying the tribes of the Mongolian–Manchurian grassland in response to the loss of Xiongnu pasture lands to invading Qin forces commanded by Meng Tian in 215 BCE.

seven-league-boots.overview: Seven-league boots are an element in European folklore. The boots allow the person wearing them to take strides of seven leagues per step, resulting in great speed. The boots are often presented by a magical character to the protagonist to aid in the completion of a significant task. From the context of English language, "seven-league boots" originally arose as a translation from the French bottes de sept lieues, popularised by Charles Perrault's fairy tales. Mentions of the legendary boots are found in: France – Charles Perrault's "Hop o' My Thumb"; Madame d'Aulnoy's "The Bee and the Orange Tree"; Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time.

shield-of-heracles.overview: The Shield of Heracles (Ancient Greek: Ἀσπὶς Ἡρακλέους, Aspis Hērakleous) is an archaic Greek epic poem that was attributed to Hesiod during antiquity. The subject of the poem is the expedition of Heracles and Iolaus against Cycnus, the son of Ares, who challenged Heracles to combat as Heracles was passing through Thessaly. It is generally dated from the end of the 7th to the middle of the 6th century BCE.

virgo.overview: Virgo (♍︎; Ancient Greek: Παρθένος, romanized: Parthénos; Latin for "virgin" or "maiden") is the sixth astrological sign in the zodiac. It spans the 150–180th degree of the zodiac. Under the tropical zodiac, the Sun transits this area between August 24 and September 23 on average. Depending on the system of astrology, individuals born during these dates may be called Virgos or Virgoans. The sign is associated with Astraea, a figure from Greek mythology. Astraea was the last immortal to abandon Earth at the end of the Silver Age when the gods fled to Olympus, which is why Virgo is associated with Earth. Astraea later became the constellation of Virgo.
